Mason’s knowledge state differs between the scenarios.

In Scenario 2, Mason knows that the financial discrepancies were caused by a clerical error, not by Martha mismanaging funds. He knows he wrongly suspected Martha and feels relieved but embarrassed. He therefore wants to apologize for his suspicion and make sure the report issue is clarified/corrected so the error does not continue.

In Scenario 3, Mason now believes Martha is competent, and he knows the problem is not Martha but the inadequate financial management system. His focus shifts from apologizing for a mistaken suspicion to proposing a new, more robust financial system to prevent future clerical errors.

He does not yet know how management will react to the proposal or whether it will be approved. That future event is outside his knowledge at this point.

So yes, Mason’s intention changes from Scenario 2 to Scenario 3: from apologizing and correcting/clarifying the report issue to proposing new systems.
